cases.description: Design the home timeline of a social network: hundreds of millions of users, fan-out of posts to followers, and the hot-key and freshness problems that come with it. Exercises partitioning, replication lag, and caching trade-offs.

questions.question: Before any design: how would you scope this problem? What would you ask me, and what load numbers would you establish before drawing a single box?

commonMistakes: Jumping to a technology choice (Redis, Cassandra, Kafka) before establishing any scale numbers
Treating all users as identical and never discovering the celebrity skew
Assuming real-time delivery with no stated latency bound or freshness SLO
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 names specific load parameters and the skew, then connects them to design consequences; a 3 asks a couple of generic questions like 'how many users?' and moves on without pinning down numbers.

keyPoints.point: States concrete load parameters first: daily/monthly active users, posts per second, timeline reads per second, read/write ratio, and follower-count distribution
Identifies the skewed access pattern: a tiny fraction of users (celebrities) generate a disproportionate share of fan-out work, which drives the hardest design decisions
Clarifies freshness expectations explicitly: how quickly must a post become visible, and does the poster have a stronger expectation than followers do

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer opens with clarifying questions, writes down rough numbers (e.g. posts/sec, timeline reads/sec, read/write ratio), names the two load shapes that drive the design — heavily skewed follower counts and read-dominated traffic — and states an explicit freshness target instead of assuming instant delivery.

questions.question: Walk me through your core design. What data do you store, how is it partitioned, and how does a post travel from the writer to their followers' timelines?

commonMistakes: Fan-out on read for everyone: every timeline load scans all followed users, with no discussion of the read cost
No partition key at all — 'we'll shard the database' with no scheme
No replication story: a single copy of each partition
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 justifies push vs pull with the read/write ratio and names the partition key and replication roles; a 3 describes 'store posts, query them on read' with no partitioning or replication detail.

keyPoints.point: Chooses fan-out on write (push): when a post is created, its ID is appended to each follower's timeline, justified by the read-heavy workload
Partitions timelines by follower (hash of user ID) so loading one user's timeline touches a single partition
Picks a data model deliberately for the access pattern (e.g. a per-user document or wide row giving locality for whole-timeline reads) and justifies it
Replicates each partition with a leader and followers for availability and read scaling, with writes going through the leader

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer describes a per-user timeline structure partitioned by follower ID, a write path that fans post IDs out to follower timelines (push, justified by the read/write ratio), and leader-follower replication per partition for availability — showing which component owns each concern.

questions.question: A celebrity with 50 million followers posts. Your fan-out job now has to perform 50 million writes for a single post. How do you handle this?

commonMistakes: 'Just add more machines' without addressing the single-post write amplification
Applying pull fan-out to every user, destroying read latency for the common case
Never having encountered the hot-key problem; treating it as a generic scaling issue
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 proposes the hybrid push/pull mechanism and quantifies the trade-off; a 3 says 'celebrities get special handling' with no concrete mechanism.

keyPoints.point: Names the hot-key problem: hash partitioning spreads users evenly, but one key's write amplification breaks the fan-out pipeline
Proposes the standard hybrid fix: exempt celebrities from push fan-out and serve their posts via pull (fan-out on read), merging them into followers' timelines at read time
Discusses the tail-latency cost: read-time merging adds work to every follower's timeline load, so the fix trades write amplification for read latency

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer identifies this as the hot-key (celebrity) problem, proposes the hybrid push/pull split — normal users get push fan-out, celebrities get pull with read-time merging — and states the trade-off explicitly: the write storm disappears but every timeline read pays merging cost.

questions.question: You put a cache in front of the timelines. A user posts, refreshes, and doesn't see their own post — but their friend sees it immediately. Explain what's happening and how you'd fix it.

commonMistakes: Blaming 'eventual consistency' as a magic phrase with no mechanism
'Make everything synchronous' with no discussion of what that costs
Confusing a stale read with a lost write
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 names read-your-writes, explains the mechanism, and states the cost of the fix; a 3 says 'it's a cache invalidation bug' and suggests clearing the cache.

keyPoints.point: Diagnoses a read-your-writes violation: the poster's read hit a lagging replica or stale cache entry while the friend's read landed on fresher state
Proposes concrete fixes: route the poster's reads to the leader briefly after their own write, track the write's log position, or invalidate/write-through the cache on post
States the general cost: stronger read guarantees sacrifice read scalability, since funneling reads to the leader makes it a bottleneck

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer names the anomaly (read-your-writes, caused by replication lag or a stale cache), explains the two-reads-two-replicas mechanism, gives the standard fix — read-from-leader after own writes or write-through invalidation — and notes the scalability cost of that fix.

questions.question: A regional outage takes down one of your three regions during peak traffic. Walk me through what your users experience, and tell me what you deliberately gave up to keep the service running.

commonMistakes: Assuming failover is instant and invisible to users
Claiming strong consistency and full availability at the same time during a partition
No recovery story — the region just 'comes back'
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 names the availability-over-linearizability trade-off and the recovery mechanism; a 3 says 'traffic fails over to the other regions' with no trade-off articulated.

keyPoints.point: Treats partial failure as the normal case: the remaining regions keep serving, possibly with degraded freshness, rather than the whole system going down
States the consistency trade-off explicitly: during the partition the design chooses availability (serve possibly-stale timelines) over linearizability
Describes recovery: the returning region catches up from the replication log, and any conflicting writes accepted during the outage are resolved by a stated policy

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer treats the outage as routine partial failure, names the explicit availability-over-linearizability choice during the partition, describes degraded-but-serving behavior, and covers catch-up on recovery including how conflicting writes would be resolved.

cases.scenario: You're designing the home timeline for a social network with 200 million monthly users. When someone posts, it should appear in their followers' timelines quickly. Some users have 50 million followers. I'll ask you to scope it, design the core flow, then dig into the hard parts: celebrities, caching, and regional failures.
cases.title: Social-Media Timeline Feed

cases.description: Design a rate limiter shared by a fleet of API servers: partitioned counters, the accuracy-vs-speed trade-off, clock skew in time windows, and behavior during network partitions. Exercises partitioning, consistency models, and unreliable clocks.

questions.question: How would you scope this problem? What do you need to know before you start designing?

commonMistakes: Designing before asking what happens when the limit is hit or the limiter is down
Assuming exact enforcement is required without asking
No notion of traffic shape — treating 10k/min as a flat rate
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 extracts the precision requirement and the fail-open/fail-closed policy as scoping questions; a 3 asks only about request volume.

keyPoints.point: Establishes load parameters: total requests per second, number of API keys, burst vs sustained traffic shape
Pins down the precision requirement: is occasionally admitting 10,050 requests when the limit is 10,000 acceptable, or must enforcement be exact
Clarifies failure behavior: when the limiter itself is down or unreachable, do requests fail open (allowed) or fail closed (rejected)

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer asks about scale, burstiness, and key cardinality, then asks the two questions that shape everything: how exact enforcement must be, and whether the limiter fails open or closed — because those answers decide how much coordination the design can afford.

questions.question: Design the counting mechanism. Hundreds of servers need to enforce a per-key limit with no single bottleneck — how do requests get counted?

commonMistakes: A single global counter or single Redis instance as the design's core
Purely local per-server counters with no cross-server aggregation story
Partitioning with no stated partition key
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 names the partition key, the single-writer-per-partition rule, and the replication story; a 3 says 'shard the counters' with no key and no write-serialization story.

keyPoints.point: Partitions counters by hashing the API key, so each key's count lives on exactly one partition and increments never need cross-partition coordination
Uses a single leader (or owner) per counter partition to serialize increments for that key
Replicates each counter partition so the limiter survives node failures without losing enforcement state

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer partitions counters by hash of the API key, gives each partition a single writer that serializes increments, replicates partitions for fault tolerance, and explains why this removes the bottleneck: servers route a key's check to its owning partition instead of contending on shared state.

questions.question: Two servers each observe half of one key's traffic within the same second. How do you keep the count correct — and how much accuracy are you willing to trade for speed?

commonMistakes: Assuming partitioned counters are automatically exact
'Just use a distributed lock per request' with no latency analysis
Hand-waving the accuracy question instead of stating a concrete error budget
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 quantifies the trade-off with an explicit error budget and ties it to the coordination cost; a 3 says 'it'll be approximately right' without saying how approximate or why.

keyPoints.point: Recognizes that an exact global count requires linearizable increments — synchronous coordination on every request — and names that cost
Notes that quorum-style reads give probable freshness, not exactness: concurrent increments can still be missed
Proposes the practical compromise explicitly tied to the scoping answer: partitioned authoritative counters plus a small over-admission budget, or asynchronous aggregation with bounded error

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer states the core tension — exactness demands per-request coordination, which costs latency — and proposes a deliberate compromise (authoritative per-key partition with an explicit over-admission budget, or bounded-error async aggregation), justified by the precision requirement established in scoping.

questions.question: Your time windows are time-based, but clocks across your fleet disagree by hundreds of milliseconds. What breaks, and how do you handle it?

commonMistakes: 'We'll sync clocks with NTP' as the complete answer, ignoring that NTP is only approximate
Using timestamps from different servers to order requests exactly
Not seeing any problem with clocks at all
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 explains the boundary-double-count mechanism and removes cross-node clock dependence; a 3 says 'clock skew could cause issues' and suggests NTP.

keyPoints.point: Explains the breakage: wall clocks jump and disagree, so window boundaries differ per server — requests near a boundary get double-counted or dropped depending on which server's clock you ask
Uses monotonic clocks for measuring elapsed time and local timeouts, never wall-clock time for cross-node decisions
Designs the algorithm to not depend on cross-node clock agreement — e.g. the owning partition's clock defines the window, or windows are approximate by design

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer identifies skewed wall clocks as the culprit behind inconsistent window edges, prescribes monotonic clocks for local elapsed-time measurement, and removes the dependence on cross-node agreement — for example, the partition owning a key is the authority on its window boundaries.

questions.question: A network partition splits your datacenters: both sides keep receiving API traffic. What does your rate limiter do — and is that the right call?

commonMistakes: Assuming the partition is detectable and both sides just 'coordinate'
Claiming exact enforcement continues normally during the split
Choosing fail-open or fail-closed with no business justification
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 names the trade-off, picks a concrete partition policy, and justifies it in business terms; a 3 says 'the limiter keeps working' without explaining how or at what cost.

keyPoints.point: Applies partition reasoning: a side cut off from the others cannot know whether it is the majority, so it must decide from local information alone
States the CAP-style choice explicitly: strict global accuracy and availability cannot both hold during the partition, so one is sacrificed deliberately

Proposes a concrete policy and defends it in business terms: e.g. each side enforces against a pre-split budget share (available, may over-admit) vs the minority side fails closed (accurate, rejects legitimate traffic)

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer reasons from the partition: neither side knows the global count, so it picks an explicit policy — for example, splitting the budget across sides ahead of time so both stay available with bounded over-admission — and defends it by comparing the business cost of over-admission against rejecting legitimate traffic.

cases.scenario: You're building a rate limiter for a public API: each API key is allowed 10,000 requests per minute. Traffic arrives through hundreds of stateless API servers spread across three datacenters. I'll ask you to scope it, design the counting, then push on accuracy, clocks, and partitions.
cases.title: Distributed Rate Limiter

cases.description: Design a payment ledger where money moves between accounts exactly once despite aggressive client retries, crashes, and concurrent transfers. Exercises transactions, isolation levels, idempotence, and distributed commit.

questions.question: Scope this for me. What makes a payment ledger different from a generic CRUD service, and what do you need to pin down before designing?

commonMistakes: Treating a transfer as two independent single-row updates
Missing retries entirely — designing for the happy path only
No mention of auditability despite the regulatory framing
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 names multi-object atomicity and retry-driven idempotence as scoping outputs; a 3 asks about transfer volume and moves on.

keyPoints.point: Identifies the multi-object atomicity requirement: a transfer debits one account and credits another, and both updates must succeed or fail together
sections: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction

keyPoints.point: Establishes load parameters (transfers per second, account count) and the retry-heavy client behavior that makes idempotence mandatory
Frames correctness as end-to-end: broker-level guarantees alone don't help if a retry can double-apply a transfer downstream

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer names the transfer as a multi-object atomic operation, quantifies the load, calls out aggressive retries as a first-class requirement (not an edge case), and frames correctness end-to-end — the ledger, the clients, and the downstream consumers all have to agree on exactly-once.

questions.question: Design the transfer operation. A client may retry the same transfer five times after timeouts — how do you guarantee the money moves exactly once?

commonMistakes: 'Check if it exists, then insert' as two separate steps with a race between them
Relying on the client to not retry, or on timeouts never happening
Reaching for two-phase commit across services for a single transfer
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 puts the idempotency key inside the same atomic transaction and explains why that closes the race; a 3 says 'use idempotency keys' without saying where they're stored or what makes the check atomic.

keyPoints.point: Wraps debit and credit in a single atomic transaction so a crash or retry can never leave a half-applied transfer; aborted work is discarded and safe to retry
sections: The Slippery Concept of a Transaction

keyPoints.point: Makes retries safe with idempotency: a deterministic idempotency key stored in the same transaction, so a repeated request is recognized as a duplicate, not a new transfer
Keeps the commit local to one system and uses idempotent downstream operations, rather than reaching for a distributed transaction across services

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer puts the debit, the credit, and the idempotency-key record inside one local transaction, so any retry with the same key is deduplicated and any crash leaves nothing half-written — achieving exactly-once effects without a distributed transaction.

questions.question: Two transfers debit the same account at the same time. What isolation level do you run, and exactly which anomaly are you preventing?

commonMistakes: 'Use transactions' as if any transaction level prevents this
Claiming read committed prevents lost updates
Choosing serializable with no awareness of the performance cost or SSI abort retries
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 traces the lost-update interleaving step by step and names why the chosen level fixes it; a 3 says 'use a higher isolation level' without naming the anomaly.

keyPoints.point: Names the lost-update anomaly: both transactions read balance 100, both subtract 60, both write back 40 — 60 units vanish
Explains why read committed is not enough: it prevents dirty reads/writes but does not stop two transactions from overwriting each other's updates
Chooses a real defense — serializable isolation (or SSI with application retries), atomic compare-and-set updates, or explicit row locking — and can say what it costs

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer walks through the lost-update interleaving concretely, explains why read committed permits it, and picks a defense (serializable/SSI with retry handling, or atomic conditional writes) while acknowledging the throughput cost of stronger isolation.

questions.question: The ledger must update and the fraud-detection service must record the transfer. Walk me through your options for making both happen atomically — and tell me what you'd actually ship.

commonMistakes: Choosing 2PC with no mention of the blocking-coordinator failure mode
'Call the fraud service, then commit the ledger' as if ordering the calls solves atomicity
No consumer-side idempotence story — at-least-once delivery alone doesn't give exactly-once effects
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 compares all three options, names 2PC's blocking failure, and closes the loop with idempotent consumers; a 3 picks the outbox pattern by name without explaining why the alternatives fail.

keyPoints.point: Describes two-phase commit honestly: prepare then commit/abort, but the coordinator is a single point of failure and crashed coordinators leave participants blocked holding locks
Rejects naive dual writes: if the ledger commits and the fraud-service call fails, the two systems silently diverge with no reliable recovery

Ships the practical pattern: transactional outbox (event written in the same local transaction, relayed afterward) or CDC from the replication log, with an idempotent consumer — at-least-once delivery plus idempotence gives exactly-once effects

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer compares 2PC (correct but operationally painful: blocking coordinator failures), dual writes (simple but silently divergent), and the transactional outbox/CDC pattern — then ships the outbox, explaining that at-least-once delivery combined with an idempotent fraud-service consumer yields exactly-once effects end to end.

questions.question: Regulators demand one authoritative ordering of all transfers — a single sequence everyone agrees on. How do you provide it, and what does it cost you?

commonMistakes: Sorting by wall-clock timestamps across servers as the ordering mechanism
Claiming total order with no single point of serialization and no cost
Keeping only current balances with no auditable history
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 names the sequencer, states its throughput/latency cost, and connects the log to auditing via event sourcing; a 3 says 'we'll order by timestamp'.

keyPoints.point: Provides total order via a single sequencer: one leader's log (or consensus-ordered log) assigns every transfer a sequence number, so all replicas see the same order
States the price: ordering guarantees need synchronous coordination, adding latency to every write and creating a throughput bottleneck at the sequencer
Keeps the append-only event log as the audit trail itself: event sourcing gives regulators full history and replayability, not just the current balances

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer funnels transfers through a single ordered log (leader sequencer or consensus), is honest that this serializes writes and adds latency, and points out the log doubles as the regulator's audit trail via event sourcing — current state is derived, history is the truth.

cases.scenario: You're designing the ledger for a payments company. Transfers move money between accounts, clients retry aggressively after timeouts, and regulators audit every cent. Money must never be created, destroyed, or moved twice. I'll ask you to scope it, design the transfer itself, then dig into concurrency, cross-service commit, and the audit trail.
cases.title: Exactly-Once Payment Ledger

cases.description: Design a key-value store spanning three regions with tunable consistency: replication topologies, quorum math, conflict resolution after partitions, and zero-downtime region expansion. Exercises replication, partitioning, and consensus.

questions.question: Scope it. What do you need to establish before choosing any replication strategy?

commonMistakes: Designing for 'strong consistency everywhere' without asking what the product actually needs
No per-region traffic numbers — treating three regions as identical
Skipping the why-replicate question entirely
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 segments data by consistency need during scoping; a 3 asks about scale and picks a single consistency level for everything.

keyPoints.point: Establishes load parameters: key count, value sizes, reads vs writes per second, and per-region traffic split
States why replication is wanted at all: lower latency for nearby users, surviving regional failures, and scaling read throughput
Extracts the real consistency requirement per data class instead of accepting one global answer — which data can be stale and which cannot

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer quantifies the workload, names the three reasons for replicating (latency, availability, read scale), and refuses a one-size-fits-all consistency answer — it segments the data by how much staleness each class tolerates, because that segmentation drives the whole design.

questions.question: Three regions. Pick a replication topology, tell me where writes go, and defend the choice.

commonMistakes: Single global leader with no discussion of cross-region write latency
Multi-leader with no conflict-resolution policy
Conflating partitioning and replication — 'we shard across regions'
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 defends multi-leader with the latency argument and states its conflict policy in the same breath; a 3 picks a topology without saying where writes go or what conflicts cost.

keyPoints.point: Chooses multi-leader (one leader per region) so each region accepts local writes with low latency, replicating asynchronously to the other regions
Names the price up front: concurrent writes to the same key in different regions create conflicts that must be detected and resolved
Keeps partitioning and replication as independent choices: data is partitioned within each region for scale and replicated across regions for latency/availability

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer picks multi-leader with a leader per region for local-write latency, describes the async cross-region replication flow, states the conflict-resolution policy as part of the choice (not an afterthought), and separates the partitioning scheme from the replication topology.

questions.question: The product team first demands read-your-writes globally, then admits most data is fine eventual — but billing keys must be strongly consistent. What consistency offering do you actually build?

commonMistakes: One consistency level for the entire store
Promising linearizability everywhere with no latency discussion
Treating quorum reads as equivalent to linearizability
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 tiers the offering and prices each tier; a 3 says 'we'll support tunable consistency' without saying what the knobs are or what they cost.

keyPoints.point: Explains read-your-writes honestly: serve the writer's reads from the leader (or track the write's log position) and notes it costs read scalability
Offers tunable quorums for the middle ground: W + R > N makes reads probably fresh, while being explicit that quorums are not linearizability
Reserves true linearizability — synchronous cross-region coordination — for the billing keys only, and quotes its latency price openly

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer builds a tiered offering: eventual by default, read-your-writes via leader reads where the scalability cost is acceptable, tunable quorums for the middle, and full linearizability quarantined to the billing keys with an explicit latency price — matched to the segmented requirements from scoping.

questions.question: The US and EU regions both accept writes to the same key while the transatlantic link is down. The link heals. Walk me through exactly what happens next.

commonMistakes: 'The latest write wins' with no definition of latest and no clock-skew awareness
Assuming conflicts can't happen because 'we have replication'
No mechanism for even detecting that a conflict occurred
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 walks the heal sequence mechanically and names the LWW clock-skew trap; a 3 says 'conflicts get resolved' without a detection or resolution mechanism.

keyPoints.point: Describes conflict detection: version vectors (or equivalent) reveal the two writes as concurrent rather than causally ordered once the regions reconnect
Walks through the chosen resolution policy mechanically — e.g. last-write-wins applies one value and discards the other, a merge function combines them, or the application is asked
Flags the last-write-wins trap: resolving by wall-clock timestamp can silently discard the genuinely later write when clocks disagree

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer narrates the heal step by step — reconnection, version-vector comparison exposing concurrency, then the resolution policy applied mechanically — and explicitly warns that timestamp-based last-write-wins can silently lose data under clock skew.

questions.question: Last one: you need to add a fourth region with zero downtime and no data loss. How?

commonMistakes: Hash-mod-N rebalancing that moves nearly all data
A maintenance window with downtime as the plan
Cutting traffic over before the new region has converged
rubric.fiveVsThree: A 5 gives the ordered runbook with the minimal-movement argument and a convergence check; a 3 says 'we'll rebalance the shards' with no sequence.

keyPoints.point: Uses consistent hashing for the handover: the new region takes over key ranges from its neighbors so only nearby data moves — and explicitly avoids hash-mod-N, which would remap nearly every key
Keeps serving during the move: the new region first catches up as a non-serving replica (snapshot plus replication log) before taking traffic
Treats the expansion as routine partial-membership change: verifies convergence (e.g. anti-entropy comparison) before cutting reads over, and keeps writes available throughout

rubric.strongAnswer: A great answer gives an ordered runbook: join as a catching-up replica, stream snapshot plus live log, hand over hash ranges with minimal data movement, verify convergence before serving reads, and never block writes — treating region expansion as a normal membership change, not a migration event.

cases.scenario: You're designing a multi-region key-value store for a global SaaS product: three regions — US, EU, Asia — single-digit-millisecond reads in each region, and the product team keeps changing its mind about how consistent reads need to be. I'll ask you to scope it, pick a replication topology, then push on consistency knobs, write conflicts, and adding a fourth region.
cases.title: Multi-Region Key-Value Store
